Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Israel’s election remains deadlocked: with most votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc leads but is short of a majority, prompting coalition speculation and warnings against inflaming allegations of interference. 
• Xi Jinping steps up party purges under the anti-corruption banner, seen by observers as consolidating authority ahead of key political meetings. 
• Alaska’s governor ordered a probe into alleged Democrat-linked “same-name” spoiler candidates; Trump urged barring a Democratic Senate contender amid mounting scrutiny. 
• Canada and the EU pursue deeper economic and defence ties at a Montreal summit as Europe advances a Pan‑Arctic undersea cable bypassing the U.S., while the FCC tightens curbs on Chinese tech imports. 
• Vietnam signed the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition on peaceful space exploration; Brazil’s Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami amid investigations at home. 
Why it matters: Political fragmentation, great‑power discipline campaigns, and technology decoupling are reshaping alliances, elections, and the rules of engagement in both geopolitics and the global tech ecosystem.

• AI-enabled drones are accelerating in Ukraine, with officials warning AI could drive battlefield decisions as early as next year. 
• Ethiopia acquired Russian fighter jets and air defences amid renewed fighting in Tigray, signalling external rearmament in a live conflict. 
• A hacker breached DHS systems, exposing data of over 41,000 employees; in Israel, a caretaker period could still see escalation against Iran, analysts say. 
Why it matters: Safety lapses, AI’s militarization, regional rearmament, and cyber vulnerabilities each heighten the risk of miscalculation and harm beyond battlefields.

• ECB chief Christine Lagarde will step down early; markets eye Europe’s energy interventions and fragile U.S. GDP growth; worker engagement sank to its lowest since 2011. 
Why it matters: AI investment recalibration, leadership shifts at central banks, consolidation in consumer tech logistics, and energy‑cost pressures are steering market sentiment ahead of elections.

Climate & Environment
• Scientists warn climate models undercount dangerous feedback loops and call for WHO to declare climate change a public health emergency.

• Impacts intensify: historic high tides inundated California; cyclone Arnab struck India; satellites tracked an Antarctic iceberg’s escape. 
• Policy shifts: Trump moved to terminate methane rules; the UK budget laid out energy measures; cities drive a green investment boom; Africa seeks a stronger adaptation finance focus at COP31. 
• Conservation efforts raised nearly $20m to protect Queensland land; Menindee Lakes hit five‑year lows amid fish‑kill risks. 
Why it matters: Managing escalating climate impacts while accelerating clean transitions hinges on policy coherence, finance, and rapid deployment of technologies and nature‑based solutions.

Society & Human Rights.title: ASICS' Life-Sized Diorama Offered a Window Into a New Human Species
Society & Human Rights.text: With its founding philosophy, a Sound Mind in a Sound Body, ASICS has stood as an unwavering champion of movement for the mind. Feeding into events and activations, this year on World Mental Health Day, the brand installed a life-sized diorama in Paris showing its commitment to tackling issues humanity faces today. Boxed in a see-through case, the diorama centered on a realistic human model, sitting in a familiar position in front of screens, immobile and hunched over. From a global study stating 86% of people surveyed spend their waking hours inactive, it captured one of the most widespread modern behaviors. ASICS presented the model as part of a new species it calls Homo Scrollus Canapus. Though it takes a humorous side, the installation adopted a museum format with explanatory labels and documentary-style voiceovers to engage those passing by. Hypebeast visited the forecourt of Grande Halle de La Villette, which housed the diorama for two days. Positioned in the middle of a high-traffic area, we went on the ground to catch individuals as they interacted with the installation. The video shows all walks of life observing the model and sharing personal stories of the modern-day habits that have quietly designed movement out of our lives, like doomscrolling, binge-watching, and prolonged hours in front of computer screens.The diorama, however, wasn’t just a warning of the new species. It gave onlookers a solution to kicking their restless slump to the curb. On one side of the installation, a board noted that dedicating a few minutes to movement can boost your mind and body. These insights were championed by its 15 Minutes to Thrive challenge. Aiming to encourage everyday activity, we gathered perspectives on the initiative in a dedicated Ask the Community installment. Artificial Intelligence.title: Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI
Artificial Intelligence.text: Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.The problem, not the titleEngineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.The importance of systems thinkingSystems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.Human judgment is importantAI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.IEEE’s vital roleThe broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.A larger definition of the engineerAI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Science & Technology.title: How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight
Science & Technology.text: In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the  Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” says Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.” At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta TechnologiesThis ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.To that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta says its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO“We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.Reducing the Risk of FAA CertificationBeta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.Beta Technologies, Made in VermontAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.That helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.Beta’s Approach to BatteriesIn Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.   Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta TechnologiesBy contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them big. This limitation is from the batteries.”In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.Beta Technologies’ Electric EcosystemWhat sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions. Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta TechnologiesFurther evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the company’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.Then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

Entertainment.text: SummaryTony Gilroy has unveiled the official trailer for Behemoth! starring Pedro Pascal as a cellist scoring films in Los AngelesThe nonlinear narrative features original compositions from nine acclaimed composers including Michael Giacchino and Alan SilvestriThe ensemble cast stars Olivia Wilde alongside Will Arnett and Matthew Lillard marking Gilroy's first feature film in 14 yearsFilmmaker Tony Gilroy has officially unveiled the trailer for his upcoming drama Behemoth!, starring Pedro Pascal as a classical cellist returning to Los Angeles to score motion pictures. The project marks the director’s first feature film in 14 years following a celebrated reception at the New York Film Festival.The formally ambitious, character-driven narrative chronicles two decades in the life of cellist Alex Serian (Pascal), exploring the unresolved reasons behind his departure and return. Constructed around a nonlinear, music-led framework where musical cues trigger memories spanning 20 years, the film consistently intercuts between live orchestral performances and Alex’s real life. Rather than serving as passive background accompaniment, the score functions as an active narrative device reflecting his personal turning points.To establish the film's complex musical architecture, Gilroy enlisted nine distinct composers—Michael Giacchino, Alan Silvestri, James Newton Howard, Michael Abels, Henry Jackman, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Nami Melumad, and Brandon Roberts—each scoring a different fictional movie within the story. The ensemble cast features Olivia Wilde, Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Will Arnett, and Matthew Lillard, arriving as Gilroy’s first feature since 2012’s The Bourne Legacy and his acclaimed tenure helming Andor.Behemoth! premieres in theaters on December 4.Read more at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Prada's Holiday 2026 Campaign Turns Into a Hand-Drawn Winter Fairytale
Entertainment.text: SummaryPrada unveils its Holiday 2026 campaign, “Drawing Prada.”Maya Hawke, Sadie Sink and other actors star in whimsical, hand-illustrated worlds.Animator John Pomeroy and photographer Glen Luchford blend live action with traditional animation.Prada is bringing the magic of traditional animation into the holiday season with its Holiday 2026 campaign, titled “Drawing Prada.” Blurring the boundaries between reality and imagination, the campaign transforms the House's festive narrative into a series of whimsical, hand-illustrated worlds that evoke the charm of classic Hollywood cinema and childhood storybooks.Under the creative direction of Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, the project celebrates the art of storytelling through an intentionally nostalgic medium, placing hand-drawn animation at the center of its visual identity. Leading the creative process is legendary animator John Pomeroy, whose decades-long career has helped shape some of cinema's most recognizable animated productions at studios such as Disney. His team of artists brings fantastical winter landscapes and playful animal characters to life, reinforcing the campaign's emphasis on craftsmanship, human expression and the enduring appeal of stories passed between generations.The campaign features an ensemble of rising and established acting talent, including Chen Haoyu, Luther Ford, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Maya Hawke and Sadie Sink. Each appears within an imaginative setting where live-action photography merges with illustrated scenery, creating dreamlike compositions that feel suspended between a cinematic frame and a hand-painted storybook. Shot by Glen Luchford, the campaign carefully aligns lighting and perspective with the surrounding illustrations, allowing the real and imagined elements to coexist within the same visual space.Across a series of still images and short footage, the cast encounters whimsical wintertime scenes and fantastical environments, where the contrast between contemporary figures and traditional animation lends the imagery a distinctly surreal quality. The result is a playful interpretation of the holiday season that draws on the warmth of familiar festive imagery while celebrating the artistry behind its creation.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: 'Pokémon Unite' to Officially Shut Down in March 2027
Entertainment.text: SummaryThe Pokémon Company has announced that 'Pokémon Unite' will officially conclude service on March 23 2027Developed with TiMi Studios the five-on-five MOBA has halted gem purchases and auto-renewals ahead of a final farewell event in NovemberA newly introduced Library feature will allow players to download and view select in-game items locally before servers go offlineThe Pokémon Company has confirmed that Pokémon Unite will officially shut down in March 2027. The five-on-five multiplayer online battle arena title will close its servers on March 23, 2027, at 00:00 UTC (March 22 at 8:00 PM ET), concluding a nearly six-year live-service run.Developed alongside Tencent’s TiMi Studios, the free-to-play MOBA originally launched on Nintendo Switch in July 2021 before rolling out to mobile devices with full cross-platform matchmaking. The impending shutdown follows an earlier indication in July, when The Pokémon Company removed the title from the 2027 Pokémon World Championships in favor of an independent Tokyo tournament that will begin qualifiers this December.With the closure announced, in-game sales of gems, new Unite Club memberships, and subscription auto-renewals have been terminated immediately. Players can continue spending previously acquired gems until the final cutoff, and existing memberships will remain active through their standard expiration dates. A final update featuring a farewell event is scheduled for November 12, alongside a new Library feature allowing users to locally download and view select in-game inventory before the servers permanently go dark.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: PlayStation Revives '90s Transparent Tech Aesthetic With the “Prism Collection”
Entertainment.text: SummaryPlayStation unveils its Prism Collection of translucent DualSense controllers and matching PS5 covers.Flare Orange, Emerald Green and Graphite Gray revive nostalgic '90s gaming aesthetics.Launching February 4, 2027, controllers cost around $85 USD, with preorders beginning November 10, 2026.Transparent gaming hardware is making a comeback as PlayStation revisits one of the most recognizable design trends of the late 1990s with its new Prism Collection. The latest lineup introduces three translucent colorways for the DualSense wireless controller and matching PlayStation 5 console covers, offering a nostalgic yet futuristic interpretation of Sony's current-generation hardware.Available in Flare Orange, Emerald Green and Graphite Gray, each design features a high-gloss, see-through shell that offers a glimpse of the technology beneath. Flare Orange delivers a vibrant finish that takes on subtle rosy tones where the transparent materials overlap, while Emerald Green adopts a deeper hunter-green hue with a silky appearance. Graphite Gray offers a more understated alternative, pairing a cool-toned, smoky exterior with the collection's glossy finish.Across all three designs, a contrasting metallic center panel brings a refined touch to the controllers, balancing their exposed internal details with the PS5's streamlined industrial aesthetic. According to PlayStation's Color, Material and Finish design team, the collection was developed in response to fans' enthusiasm for the return of transparent controllers, drawing inspiration from the see-through electronics that defined gaming culture in the late '90s.The Prism Collection is scheduled to launch globally starting February 4, 2027, with regional availability varying by market. DualSense controllers are priced at $85 USD each, while matching console covers retail for $75 USD. Preorders begin November 10, 2026, in participating markets, with the collection available through PlayStation Direct where supported and select retailers.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Kobe Bryant's Game-Worn, Dual-Signed Air Jordan 8 Lakers PE Hits the Auction Block
Entertainment.text: SummaryThe Realest has officially opened the auction for Kobe Bryant's game-worn and dual-signed Air Jordan 8 Lakers Player Exclusive sneakersSourced from Bryant's celebrated 2002–03 sneaker free agency season the pair features his signature and number 8 inscription across the strapsIndependently photomatched by MeiGray and SIA the size 14 sneakers are open for bidding alongside his 2003–04 game-worn jersey through November 8The Realest has officially launched the auction for Kobe Bryant's game-worn, dual-signed Air Jordan 8 Lakers Player Exclusive sneakers. Sourced from the Black Mamba's historic 2002–03 sneaker free agency era, the rare footwear reaches the auction block following the platform’s international Gold Label Grails World Tour.Worn during the Los Angeles Lakers’ 104–96 victory over the Boston Celtics on March 21, 2003, the size 14 pair comes finished in the franchise’s signature purple, gold, and white palette. Bryant logged 13 points, seven assists, and three rebounds during the matchup at STAPLES Center, leaving behind distinct in-game wear along with the original laces and insoles. Both sneakers feature Bryant’s personal signature and his iconic "No. 8" inscription written in black marker across the model’s hallmark criss-cross straps. The artifact has been independently photomatched by both MeiGray and Sports Investors Authentication (SIA).The sneakers arrive alongside Bryant’s signed, game-worn No. 8 Lakers jersey from the 2003–04 season, which has already surpassed $712,000 USD in active bidding. Prior to the sale, both items traveled across Los Angeles and premier Asian destinations including Hong Kong, Tokyo, and Beijing, stopping at Mutianyu on the Great Wall of China and the Bird’s Nest National Stadium.Bidding on Kobe Bryant’s game-worn Air Jordan 8 Lakers Player Exclusives and his 2003–04 game-worn jersey closes on November 8, 2026, exclusively via TheRealest.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
